processing: As with other Yunnan raw pu-erh, the leaf is typically wilted, wok-fired, rolled and sun-dried into mao cha, then sold loose or steamed and pressed; no ripe-style pile fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as is usual for Mengku raw pu-erh; little is documented about the season here beyond that.
appearance_dry: Long, dark strands, typically with a slightly wild look compared with cultivated Mengku leaf.
appearance_wet: Thick dark leaves, varied in shape, as is usual for wild-tree material.
taste_profile: Full and sweet on entry with a osmanthus-like scent left in the cup; a quick mouth-watering effect and a strong, long aftertaste, with some early bitterness in some lots.

brewing.notes: Treat it with caution: it is potent, and young tea from these trees is not advised in quantity. Use less leaf if you are unused to wild tea.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, typically spring, and described as a tea for long storage rather than heavy drinking when young. Modern brands use the name for ordinary cakes too, some of them ripe, so a Daxueshan label does not by itself mean wild trees. Ask for tree type and location.
description:
Daxueshan, Big Snow Mountain, is the ridge dividing Mengku's eastern and western half-mountains in Shuangjiang County, Lincang. In tea it usually means leaf linked to the wild-type old tea trees on its middle and upper slopes, reported at about 2,200 to 2,750 metres in forest and over more than 12,000 mu.

The trees are described as a wild Dali type. Picked leaf goes through the normal raw method, as far as is recorded; the difference lies in the plant, and that is also why it needs some care.

Accounts give an orange-yellow cup with an osmanthus-like scent, a full sweet entry, strong aftertaste and real potency. Trade descriptions warn against drinking much of it young, and they favour keeping it. Start small and short.

The name is not protected. Yunnan has other Daxueshan tea areas, including Yongde, and brands use the name freely for cultivated leaf and even ripe tea. Ask which mountain, and whether the trees are truly wild.

If you try it, compare it with ordinary Mengku raw tea from the slopes below. The contrast shows what the plant type does.
history:
This wild tree population is often cited as evidence for Yunnan's role in the origin of tea, but those claims come mainly from trade and local sources; no discovery date is well documented. The largest tree, the First Ancient Tea Tree, is reported at about 16.8 metres tall and is claimed to be over 2,700 years old, an age that should be read as a claim.

In the trade's Mengku Eighteen Villages grouping, Daxueshan is listed with the western half-mountain as a wild old-tree community.
